newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss support for humanitarian fund waning -survey.
newsitem.headline: Swiss support for humanitarian fund waning -survey.

text.p: Public support is waning for the government's plan for a seven billion franc ($5 billion) humanitarian foundation intended to dispel allegations that Switzerland is still hoarding profits from its World War Two dealings with Nazi Germany.

According to a survey published on Sunday, 48 percent of Swiss surveyed still approve the plan to sell part of the country's gold reserves and use the proceeds to aid victims of poverty, disasters and the Holocaust at home and abroad.
That was down from 58 percent support the same poll found when Swiss President Arnold Koller announced the surprise plan in March,, said the survey published in SonntagsBlick.
Another seven percent would approve if the foundation restricted its help to people in Switzerland, up from four percent in March.
The number of people against the plan, which faces a popular referendum next year, rose to 35 percent from 31 percent. Ten percent had no opinion, up from seven percent.
The IPSO polling agency questioned 600 people on June 11 and 12 and said its findings were accurate within four percentage points.
"Support for the Solidarity Foundation is indeed sinking. But the idea is not dead yet," the newspaper said in an accompanying story.

In an editorial, it urged the government to take a more active line to push the foundation, which was proposed as the country faced an international public relations disaster from renewed investigation into its role as a neutral financial centre during World War Two.

"The government has to wake up," columnist Juerg Lehmann wrote. "It has to anchor firmly the foundation in people's heads as a Swiss contribution to the world. It still has a chance, but it has to act. Soon it will be too late."

Support for the plan has been slipping amid sniping from right-wing politicians who say the Swiss are caving in to foreign blackmail. A survey in the L'Illustre magazine last month found 43 percent opposed and only 40 percent in favour.
This was a far cry from the majorities of 50 to 70 percent that backed the idea when Koller first proposed it.
Next year's referendum is shaping up as a watershed event in Swiss domestic politics and foreign relations.
Proponents of the fund say it would show Swiss gratitude that the tiny neutral land escaped the horrors of World War Two although surrounded by the Axis.

Opponents call it an ill-considered sell-off of national treasure in the face of pressure from foreign critics like U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato and Jewish groups who accuse Swiss banks of hoarding the unclaimed assets of Holocaust victims.
The drumbeat of criticism from abroad is helping opponents whip up opposition to the plan by appealing to Swiss national pride and sovereignty.

To help make the scheme more politically palatable, Jewish groups have already suggested dropping any reference to Holocaust victims as recipients of largesse from the foundation and paying them instead from a separate memorial fund.
Swiss banks, other private businesses and the Swiss National Bank are putting up 265 million francs in that fund to alleviate the suffering of needy Holocaust survivors and their families.

But splitting off the foundation from the Holocaust debate would make it harder for the government and business to hold up the plan as something Switzerland is doing to make amends for its controversial wartime role.

The foundation plan calls for re-valuing official gold reserves -- now on the central bank's books at less than a third of their market value -- by 14 billion francs, half of which would finance the fund.
Gradually selling seven billion francs worth of gold and investing the proceeds in securities would generate around 350 million Swiss francs ($250 million) a year to distribute to recipients.
